title: Paul and women
hookLine: Paul names women co-workers, Junia, Phoebe, Prisca, and also wrote restrictions; churches read these differently
tomorrow: a letter mailed to Rome long ago: who is it addressed to now?

lines: THE THANK-YOUS TELL WHO DID THE WORK.
cards: At an awards show, the thank-yous are where you find out who actually did the work. Romans has a thank-you page. It's the last one, the easy one to skim, a list of hellos.
And the first name on it is a woman's: "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea." Paul is vouching for her to a church that hasn't met her.
Some readers think she carried the letter itself.

teach.b: Read that page slowly. Phebe has been "a succourer of many, and of myself also."
Then: "Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus," a wife and husband, her name first, who "for my life laid down their own necks."
Then Andronicus and Junia, "my fellowprisoners, who are of note among the apostles." Readers take that last phrase two ways: well known to the apostles, or noted as apostles themselves.
In Philippians Paul asks help for "those women which laboured with me in the gospel."
And Second Timothy traces a young man's faith back through two women: "which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice." That's one side of the letters.
The other side is on the page too: "Let your women keep silence in the churches," and, in First Timothy, "I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man."
Some ordain women as pastors and read the limits as words for particular churches and moments.
Others, including the Catholic and Orthodox churches and some Protestant churches, ordain only men as priests or pastors, while honoring women's service in other ways.
Whichever way a church reads it, the names stay on the page.

how: Churches read Romans 16 and the letters' lines about women in worship and study, and they differ on ordination: some ordain women as pastors, while the Catholic and Orthodox churches and some Protestant churches ordain only men.

games.q: your church is planning a thank-you breakfast for 'pastors and elders.' the woman who has run the kids' ministry for years isn't on the list. with Romans 16 in mind, what do you suggest?
o: add her by name; Paul's thank-yous name women co-workers.
leave it; Paul only thanked people with official titles.
thank 'the women' as a group, with no names.
games.why: Romans 16 thanks Phebe, Priscilla, Junia and others one by one. churches that differ on ordination can still keep that habit of naming.

practice: Say out loud the name of a woman who taught you something about faith, or about how to live: a grandmother, a teacher, a neighbor. Let the name sound in the room.
Then hold her face in mind for the sit, the way that last page holds Phebe and Priscilla.

wordCard.voice: Paul and women. Phebe, Priscilla, Junia and others named with thanks in the letters, beside lines that limit women's speaking, which churches read in different ways.

orig.note: Greek: a servant, a minister, later a deacon. Paul uses it of Phebe in Romans 16:1.

carryVoice: Here's the line: co-workers in Christ, and the last page of Romans is full of them. Sixteen hundred days, and counting.
